SOLDERING MATERIALS

To perform any soldering job correctly, a technician must be familiar with the materials at their disposal. To make a solder connection between electrical components, three things are required. - Solder - Flux - Heat source
DISCUSSION

Solder is a tin/lead alloy that acts as both an electrical and mechanical "glue" for the soldered connection. It is applied to a heated connection and melts. Once the solder has cooled it acts as a semi-permanent electrical path. There are many varieties of solder available.

The most common form of solder is called 63/37. This solder alloy is approximately 63 percent tin and 37 percent lead. There may be a small amount of other materials such as silver or copper in the solder as well. Solder typically comes as a wire roll and can be of various gauges.

The 63/37 percentage has been found to have very good heating, melting point, and conduction characteristics. Other combinations such as 50/50 or 60/40 are also available. The various types of electrical solder all look generally the same.

The first point to consider about a soldering iron is its power. The amount of heat that an iron can produce is directly proportional to its power rating. Soldering irons can have power ratings from approximately 15 watts to over 100 watts.
The type and size of the conductor will determine the power of the soldering iron to be used. Most soldering work requires an iron that has a power rating in the 20 - 50 watt range.

Once you have an iron, it is important that the correct tip is selected. The tip is important because it transfers heat to the joint. There are many types of tips available.
Slim tips are used where the minimum heat is required, such as soldering very small or thermally sensitive components.
Medium sized tips are for general soldering work. Large tips are for heating joints where there is large surface area contact.

In all cases, it is important to keep soldering tips well tinned. This is done by coating the hot tip with a thin layer of solder. The tinning action prolongs tip life, prevents pitting, and guards against corrosion.

In many cases, copper wires must be soldered within an electrical circuit. These wires are usually spliced together to form a connection, or soldered to connector terminals on a printed circuit board.
DISCUSSION
To construct a reliable wire connection, the wire should be prepared for soldering. Wire preparation is very simple and should be done routinely in any wire connection work.

To prepare wire for soldering, the insulation or coating around the wire end should be removed using a knife or wire strippers. In either case, ensure that you do not nick the wire while removing the insulation.

Wires that are to be attached to connectors should first be tinned. This is the same process as tinning a soldering iron tip, where a small amount of solder is applied as a coating on the wire end. Tinned wire is much easier to solder than bare copper.

The correct method of tinning wire is to touch the wire with the hot soldering iron tip, and once the wire is hot enough apply solder to it. The solder should melt freely and coat the wire end, but there should not be excess solder on the wire tip.

We will now look at the procedure for splicing two wires together using a "Western Union" splice. There are many methods of connecting or splicing wires together, but a "Western Union" splice is one of the best because of its electrical properties and mechanical strength.
You must begin with the two wires that are to be connected and strip approximately 2" of insulation from each. are to be connected and strip approximately 5 cm of insulation from each.
The wires for the splice should not be tinned, but the strands of each wire should be twisted together tightly and kept straight.

The wires should then be crossed as shown below, ensuring that there is enough wire on each side of the connection to wrap 5 or more turns around the other wire. is estimation is best learned through practice.

One wire is then wrapped around the other tightly and evenly, making at least 5 turns. It is important to keep this wrap as smooth as possible. If there is excess wire after 5 turns, it should be clipped off.
The other wire is now wrapped tightly and evenly around the first to complete the splice. Again, keep the wrap smooth and clip off any excess wire after at least 5 turns.

The splice is now mechanically complete, and must be soldered. Heat the entire splice using a soldering iron and apply solder along the length of the splice, covering all turns on both sides. The solder should be smooth with no bumps or spikes. Solder bumps and spikes can pierce insulation covering the joint and may cause a short-circuit.

The finished splice should be wrapped with electrical tape or heat- shrink tubing, so that there is no exposed wire. Note that the profile of a well-made "Western Union" splice is not much greater than that of a single wire.

We will now look at several types of terminals to which wires are normally connected. The first of these is the turret terminal.

Wire that is to be soldered to a turret terminal should first be tinned, then cut to the appropriate length. The length should be long enough to wrap from 180 - 270 degrees of bare wire around the turret.
It is advisable to use round needlenose pliers to form the wire so that it fits around the turret post. This prevents the wire from getting nicked by sharp plier jaw edges.
Once you attach the wire to the turret post, heat the connection on one side of the post, and apply a small amount of solder to the other side. The solder should flow around the wire.

Now let's see how a poor solder connection is corrected.e important subject that has not yet been covered is how to rework a poor solder connection.
When redoing a poor solder connection, it is important to remove all the old solder first. There are two tools useful for this they are, the solder vacuum and solder wick.

A solder vacuum or "solder sucker" can be used to remove solder. To do this, the joint must be reheated so that the solder becomes molten. The vacuum is actuated near the joint and sucks the molten solder into a chamber which can be cleaned later.
Solder Vacuum Tippm a plated-through hole

Most solder vacuums are manually set for one-shot operations. The vacuum process may have to be repeated in order to clean away all the solder. More advanced solder workstations have continuous heated vacuums which are really combined soldering irons and vacuum units.

Solder wick can also be used to clean a poor solder connection. This wick is really a roll of copper braid which draws molten solder into itself through capillary action. The braid end must be cut off and discarded when it fills with solder.
To get the best results when using solder wick, liquid flux should be used as well. This combination does an excellent job of cleaning poor connections.
To clean a joint, first apply some liquid flux to it. Next set the solder wick on the connection and heat the joint through the wick with the soldering iron.

Once the heat level becomes high enough, the molten solder of the joint will be drawn into the wick. You may need to feed more solder wick to the connection as it becomes full of solder. Do not overheat the connection or you may damage the components.
The solder wick/flux combination generally does an excellent job of removing all traces of old solder from a connection.

Once all the old solder has been removed from a connection and the connected parts are cleaned or replaced, the connection may be reattempted using the standard rules. In most reworked connections, extra liquid flux at the joint usually makes the new connection solder well.
- Do not disturb joint until solder has set and connector is cool.
